name: Omkar and Medians
description: Uh oh! Ray lost his array yet again! However, Omkar might be able to help because he thinks he has found the OmkArray of Ray's array. The OmkArray of an array $$$a$$$ with elements $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2k-1}$$$, is the array $$$b$$$ with elements $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{k}$$$ such that $$$b_i$$$ is equal to the median of $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2i-1}$$$ for all $$$i$$$. Omkar has found an array $$$b$$$ of size $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$-10^9 \leq b_i \leq 10^9$$$). Given this array $$$b$$$, Ray wants to test Omkar's claim and see if $$$b$$$ actually is an OmkArray of some array $$$a$$$. Can you help Ray? The median of a set of numbers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2i-1}$$$ is the number $$$c_{i}$$$ where $$$c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{2i-1}$$$ represents $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2i-1}$$$ sorted in nondecreasing order.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. Description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the length of the array $$$b$$$. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$$$ ($$$-10^9 \leq b_i \leq 10^9$$$) — the elements of $$$b$$$. It is guaranteed the sum of $$$n$$$ across all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output one line containing YES if there exists an array $$$a$$$ such that $$$b_i$$$ is the median of $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2i-1}$$$ for all $$$i$$$, and NO otherwise. The case of letters in YES and NO do not matter (so yEs and No will also be accepted).
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1536D — Omkar and Medians [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
